questions.stem: Let H be the orthocentre of triangle ABC. Prove that the reflection of H in side BC lies on the circumcircle of ABC.

hint.level_0: Reflect over BC and chase the angle ∠BH'C.
hint.level_1: Show ∠BH'C = 180° − ∠A, the condition for lying on the circumcircle.

solution_steps: Let H' be the reflection of H over line BC; we show H' lies on the circumcircle.
Let the altitude from A meet BC at foot D and the circumcircle again at H'. Reflection over BC fixes D and sends the ray DH to DH'.
Angle chase: ∠HBC = 90° − C (since BH ⟂ AC), and ∠H'BC = ∠H'AC subtends the same arc; one shows ∠H'BC = ∠HBC, so BC bisects ∠HBH'.
Therefore BH = BH' and H' is the reflection of H across BC. Since ∠BH'C = ∠BHC = 180° − A, H' lies on the circle through B, C subtending 180°−A, i.e. the circumcircle.
Hence the reflection of H over BC is the second intersection of the A-altitude with the circumcircle.

questions.stem: Let I be the incentre of triangle ABC and let M be the midpoint of arc BC not containing A. Prove that MB = MI = MC.

hint.level_0: M is the arc midpoint, so MB = MC and AM bisects ∠A.
hint.level_1: Compute ∠MBI and ∠MIB and show they are equal (both A/2 + B/2).

solution_steps: M is the second intersection of the A-bisector with the circumcircle, so MB = MC (equal arcs).
Consider triangle MBI. ∠MBI = ∠MBC + ∠CBI = ∠MAC + ∠B/2 (since ∠MBC = ∠MAC subtend arc MC).
But ∠MAC = ∠A/2 (AM bisects ∠A), so ∠MBI = ∠A/2 + ∠B/2.
Also ∠MIB is exterior to triangle ABI at I: ∠MIB = ∠IAB + ∠IBA = ∠A/2 + ∠B/2.
Thus ∠MBI = ∠MIB, so triangle MBI is isosceles with MB = MI. Symmetrically MC = MI, giving MB = MI = MC.

questions.stem: Prove that for a triangle with circumradius R and inradius r, the distance OI between circumcentre and incentre satisfies OI² = R² − 2Rr.

hint.level_0: Compute the power of I in the circumcircle along line AI.
hint.level_1: Use IA = r/sin(A/2) and IM = 2R sin(A/2).

solution_steps: Use the power of the incentre I with respect to the circumcircle: pow(I) = OI² − R².
Extend AI to meet the circumcircle again at M (arc midpoint of BC). Then pow(I) = −IA·IM (I is inside).
By the trident/Fact-5 lemma, IM = MB = 2R sin(A/2). Also IA = r / sin(A/2).
Hence IA·IM = (r/ sin(A/2))·(2R sin(A/2)) = 2Rr, so OI² − R² = −2Rr.
Therefore OI² = R² − 2Rr (Euler's formula); in particular R ≥ 2r.

questions.stem: Let P be a point on the circumcircle of triangle ABC. Prove that the feet of the perpendiculars from P to the three sides (lines BC, CA, AB) are collinear.

hint.level_0: Introduce the two cyclic quadrilaterals PXCY and PXBZ.
hint.level_1: Chase directed angles and use that P is on the circumcircle to merge them.

solution_steps: Let X, Y, Z be the feet of perpendiculars from P onto BC, CA, AB.
Since ∠PXC = ∠PYC = 90°, P, X, C, Y are concyclic; similarly P, X, B, Z are concyclic.
From the first circle, ∠(XY, YP) = ∠(XC, CP); from the second, ∠(ZX, XP)…; track directed angles.
Using that P lies on the circumcircle (so ∠(CA,CP)=∠(BA,BP) appropriately), one gets ∠PXY = ∠PXZ.
Hence X, Y, Z are collinear; the line is the Simson line of P.

questions.stem: Prove that for a cyclic quadrilateral ABCD, AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC.

hint.level_0: Construct K on AC with ∠ABK = ∠DBC.
hint.level_1: Get two pairs of similar triangles and add the two relations.

solution_steps: On diagonal AC choose K with ∠ABK = ∠DBC.
Then triangles ABK and DBC are similar (equal angles, since ∠BAK = ∠BDC subtend arc BC), giving AK·BD = AB·CD.
Also ∠KBC = ∠ABD, and ∠BCK = ∠BDA subtend arc AB, so triangles KBC and ABD are similar, giving KC·BD = AD·BC.
Add: (AK + KC)·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC, i.e. AC·BD = AB·CD + AD·BC.

questions.stem: Prove that the locus of points having equal power with respect to two non-concentric circles is a straight line perpendicular to the line of centres (the radical axis).

hint.level_0: Write both powers with the |X−O|²−r² formula and equate.
hint.level_1: The quadratic terms cancel, leaving a linear (line) equation.

solution_steps: Let the circles be |X−O₁|² − r₁² and |X−O₂|² − r₂² for the two powers.
Set them equal: |X−O₁|² − r₁² = |X−O₂|² − r₂².
Expand: −2X·O₁ + |O₁|² − r₁² = −2X·O₂ + |O₂|² − r₂².
This is linear in X: 2X·(O₂−O₁) = |O₂|² − |O₁|² − r₂² + r₁², a line with normal O₂ − O₁.
Hence the locus is a line perpendicular to O₁O₂.

questions.stem: Prove that the angle between the tangent to a circle at A and a chord AB equals the inscribed angle ∠ACB in the alternate segment.

hint.level_0: Introduce the diameter at A to convert the tangent into a right angle.
hint.level_1: Use the inscribed-angle theorem on chord AB.

solution_steps: Let the tangent at A and chord AB make angle θ. Draw the diameter AD from A.
The tangent ⟂ AD, so ∠DAB = 90° − θ. Also ∠ABD = 90° (angle in semicircle), so ∠ADB = θ.
Any inscribed angle ∠ACB subtending the same chord AB from the major arc equals ∠ADB = θ.
Therefore the tangent–chord angle θ equals the inscribed angle ∠ACB in the alternate segment.

questions.stem: Prove that the midpoints of the three sides and the feet of the three altitudes of a triangle lie on one circle (the nine-point circle).

hint.level_0: Work with the medial triangle and its circumcircle.
hint.level_1: Show each altitude foot sees a side of the medial triangle at 90°.

solution_steps: Let M_a, M_b, M_c be the side midpoints and H_a the foot of the altitude from A.
Let ω be the circumcircle of the medial triangle M_aM_bM_c; since M_bM_c is a midline, M_bM_c ∥ BC, hence M_bM_c ∥ M_aH_a (both M_a and H_a lie on BC).
In right triangle AH_aC the median to the hypotenuse gives M_bH_a = ½·AC, while the midline gives M_aM_c = ½·AC, so M_bH_a = M_aM_c.
Thus M_cM_bH_aM_a is an isosceles trapezium, hence cyclic, so the foot H_a lies on ω.
By the same argument the other two altitude feet lie on ω, so the three midpoints and three feet are concyclic — the nine-point circle.

questions.stem: Let M be the midpoint of a chord PQ of a circle. Two other chords AB and CD pass through M. Let AD and BC meet PQ at X and Y. Prove that M is the midpoint of XY.

hint.level_0: Put M at the origin on line PQ and use signed lengths.
hint.level_1: Pair up similar triangles and use MP·MQ = MA·MB.

solution_steps: Drop perpendiculars and use directed lengths along PQ with M as origin; set MP = MQ = a.
Let MX = x, MY = y. Using similar triangles MXA ~ MYC and MXD ~ MYB (equal inscribed angles), form ratios x/y.
Apply the intersecting-chords relation MA·MB = MC·MD = MP·MQ = a² (power of M).
Combining the similar-triangle ratios with x and y and the power relation yields x² = y² with x, y on opposite sides, so x = −y.
Hence MX = MY, i.e. M is the midpoint of XY.

questions.stem: Prove that for a fixed point P and a variable line through P meeting a circle at U, V, the product PU·PV is constant (in magnitude), equal to |OP² − R²|.

hint.level_0: Use the foot of the perpendicular from O, the midpoint of the chord.
hint.level_1: Express PF² and FU² via Pythagoras and subtract.

solution_steps: Let O, R be the centre and radius and let the line through P meet the circle at U, V.
Let F be the foot of perpendicular from O to the line; then F is the midpoint of UV and OF ⟂ UV.
PU·PV = (PF − FU)(PF + FV) = PF² − FU² (since FU = FV).
Now PF² = OP² − OF² and FU² = R² − OF² by Pythagoras in triangles OFP and OFU.
Subtracting, PU·PV = OP² − R², independent of the line — the power of P.

questions.stem: Prove that the three altitudes of a triangle are concurrent (at the orthocentre).

hint.level_0: Build the anticomplementary triangle by drawing parallels to the sides.
hint.level_1: Altitudes of ABC become perpendicular bisectors of the big triangle.

solution_steps: Through each vertex draw the line parallel to the opposite side, forming a larger triangle A'B'C'.
Then ABC is the medial triangle of A'B'C'; e.g. A is the midpoint of B'C'.
The altitude from A in ABC is perpendicular to BC, hence perpendicular to B'C' (parallel), and passes through its midpoint A — so it is the perpendicular bisector of B'C'.
Likewise the other two altitudes are the perpendicular bisectors of C'A' and A'B'.
The perpendicular bisectors of a triangle concur (at its circumcentre), so the altitudes of ABC concur.

hint.level_0: Let the bisector hit the circle again; compare the two arcs it cuts.
hint.level_1: Equal arcs give MB = MC.

Then arcs BM and MC are equal because inscribed angles ∠BAM = ∠MAC are equal.
Equal arcs ⇒ equal chords MB = MC, so M lies on the perpendicular bisector of BC.
Thus the A-bisector and the perpendicular bisector of BC meet at M on the circumcircle, the midpoint of arc BC.

questions.stem: Prove that the A-symmedian (reflection of the A-median over the A-bisector) meets BC at a point D with BD/DC = AB²/AC².

hint.level_0: Use the area/sine ratio for BD/DC and the angle swap under reflection.
hint.level_1: Eliminate the sines using the median's equal split BM = CM.

solution_steps: Let AM be the median (M midpoint BC) and AD the symmedian, reflections over the A-bisector.
Reflection over the bisector swaps the directions of AB and AC, so ∠BAD = ∠CAM and ∠CAD = ∠BAM.
Using the ratio form (areas): BD/DC = [ABD]/[ACD] = (AB·AD sin∠BAD)/(AC·AD sin∠CAD) = (AB sin∠CAM)/(AC sin∠BAM).
For the median, BM = CM gives AB sin∠BAM = AC sin∠CAM, i.e. sin∠CAM/sin∠BAM = AB/AC.
Substitute to get BD/DC = (AB/AC)·(AB/AC) = AB²/AC².

questions.stem: Prove that the perpendicular from the centre of a circle to a chord bisects the chord, and conversely the line from the centre to a chord's midpoint is perpendicular to it.

hint.level_0: Form the two right triangles OFA, OFB.
hint.level_1: Use radii equal and hypotenuse–leg congruence.

solution_steps: Let O be the centre and AB a chord with foot of perpendicular F from O.
Triangles OFA and OFB are right-angled at F with OA = OB = R (radii) and OF common.
By the hypotenuse–leg congruence, △OFA ≅ △OFB, so FA = FB; thus F is the midpoint.
Conversely, if F is the midpoint then OA = OB and FA = FB force ∠OFA = ∠OFB = 90°.

questions.stem: From an external point P, two tangents touch a circle (centre O) at X and Y. Prove PX = PY and that PO bisects ∠XPY.

hint.level_0: Radius ⟂ tangent gives two right triangles sharing hypotenuse OP.
hint.level_1: Congruent triangles give equal tangents and the bisected angle.

In right triangles OXP and OYP, OX = OY = R and OP is common.
By hypotenuse–leg, △OXP ≅ △OYP, hence PX = PY.
The congruence also gives ∠XPO = ∠YPO, so PO bisects ∠XPY.

questions.stem: In cyclic quadrilateral ABCD with diagonals meeting at P, prove that triangles APB and DPC are similar, and deduce PA·PC = PB·PD.

hint.level_0: Find equal inscribed angles subtending arc BC.
hint.level_1: AA similarity, then cross-multiply.

∠APB = ∠DPC (vertical angles).

questions.stem: Prove that in a right triangle, the midpoint of the hypotenuse is equidistant from all three vertices (it is the circumcentre).

hint.level_0: Use the circle with diameter BC (Thales' theorem).
hint.level_1: A lies on it because ∠A = 90°.

solution_steps: Let ∠A = 90° and M the midpoint of hypotenuse BC.
The circle with diameter BC passes through A, since the angle in a semicircle is 90° (Thales).
Its centre is M, the midpoint of BC, and its radius is MB = MC = BC/2.
Since A lies on this circle, MA = MB = MC; hence M is equidistant from A, B, C.

questions.stem: Prove that in a circle, two arcs are equal if and only if their chords are equal.

hint.level_0: Translate arcs to central angles.
hint.level_1: Use SAS on the two isosceles radius-triangles.

solution_steps: Let arcs AB and CD be equal, subtending central angles ∠AOB and ∠COD.
Equal arcs ⇒ equal central angles ∠AOB = ∠COD.
Triangles AOB and COD have OA=OB=OC=OD=R and equal included angle, so they are congruent (SAS).

questions.stem: Prove that cevians AD, BE, CF of triangle ABC are concurrent if and only if (BD/DC)(CE/EA)(AF/FB) = 1.

hint.level_0: Express each ratio as a ratio of triangle areas with the common point.
hint.level_1: Multiply; for the converse use a standard 'same point' uniqueness argument.

solution_steps: Assume concurrency at P. Using areas, BD/DC = [ABD]/[ACD] = [PBD]/[PCD] = [ABP]/[ACP].
Similarly CE/EA = [BCP]/[BAP] and AF/FB = [CAP]/[CBP].
Multiply the three: the area factors cancel telescopically, giving the product = 1.
Conversely, if the product is 1, let AD, BE meet at P and let CP meet AB at F'. The forward direction gives AF'/F'B equal to AF/FB, so F'=F and the cevians concur.

questions.stem: Two circles meet at X and Y. A line through X meets the circles again at A and B, and a line through Y meets them again at C and D (A,C on the first circle). Prove that AC ∥ BD.

hint.level_0: Use the two cyclic quadrilaterals sharing chord XY.
hint.level_1: Chase directed angles to compare AC and BD with XY.

solution_steps: Use directed angles mod 180°.
∠(XA, AC) = ∠(XY, YC) since A, X, Y, C are concyclic on the first circle (chord XY).
∠(XB, BD) = ∠(XY, YD) since B, X, Y, D lie on the second circle.
But C, Y, D are collinear and A, X, B are collinear, so ∠(XY,YC)=∠(XY,YD); hence ∠(line, AC) = ∠(line, BD).
Equal directed angles with the common line XA=XB imply AC ∥ BD.

But C, Y, D are collinear and A, X, B are collinear, so ∠(XY,YC)=∠(XY,YD); hence ∠(line, AC) = ∠(line, BD). Equal directed angles with the common line XA=XB imply AC ∥ BD.

questions.stem: Among all quadrilaterals with given side lengths a, b, c, d (in order), prove that the cyclic one has the largest area.

hint.level_0: Start from Bretschneider's formula for a general quadrilateral.
hint.level_1: Only the cos² term varies; minimise it.

solution_steps: For a quadrilateral with sides a,b,c,d and one pair of opposite angles summing to 2φ, the area is
Area² = (s−a)(s−b)(s−c)(s−d) − abcd·cos²φ, where s is the semiperimeter (Bretschneider's formula).
All terms except −abcd cos²φ are fixed by the side lengths.
Area is maximised when cos²φ = 0, i.e. φ = 90°, meaning opposite angles sum to 180°.
Opposite angles summing to 180° is exactly the cyclic condition; then Area = √((s−a)(s−b)(s−c)(s−d)) (Brahmagupta).
